title: The Wind Turbine: Turning Air into Power
summary: People used wind for simple jobs for thousands of years, but it took a curious American engineer named Charles Brush to turn spinning blades into real electricity.
poll: Would you rather invent a machine that uses wind, water, or sunlight to make power?

versions.title: The Wind Turbine: Turning Air into Power
versions.text:
Long ago, people used wind to help with work. Wind spun big stones. The stones ground grain. Wind also pushed sails on boats.

Later, people built a new machine. It had long blades. Wind pushed the blades. The blades would spin.

The blades sat on top of a tall tower. Being up high caught more wind. More wind meant more spin.

This machine was called a turbine. It turned wind into power. This was a new and smart idea.

Today, many turbines stand in fields. They spin all day. They make clean power from the wind. No smoke comes out.

versions.title: The Wind Turbine: Turning Air into Power

Long ago, people used wind to help with daily work. Wind spun big stones at old mills near rivers. The stones ground grain into flour. Wind also pushed sails on ships sailing across the sea.

Later, people built a brand-new kind of machine, one quite different from anything built before. It had long, flat blades shaped much like wings. Wind pushed on these blades. This made them spin steadily around.

The blades sat on top of a very tall tower, standing high above the ground. Being placed up high let them catch stronger wind than they could closer to the ground. More wind meant the blades could spin even faster than before.

This spinning machine became known as a wind turbine. It could turn the simple force of wind into power that people could use at home and at work. This was a clever and genuinely useful new idea.

Today, many tall turbines stand together in open fields and along windy coasts around the world. They spin all day and all night without stopping. They make clean power straight from the wind, with no smoke and no burning at all.

versions.title: The Wind Turbine: Turning Air into Power
versions.text:
For most of history, people used wind for only a few simple tasks. They used it to grind grain into flour. They used it to push sails on ships. No one had used wind to make the kind of power we use in homes today.

In the late 1800s, an American engineer named Charles Brush tried something new. He built a tall tower. On top he placed many long, thin blades. Wind pushed against these blades. This made them spin steadily around a central point.

Brush connected his spinning blades to a generator. A generator is a machine that turns motion into power. As the wind spun the blades, the generator made a small, steady supply of power. This power ran his own house.

Other engineers soon copied Brush's idea. They built taller towers. They built longer, more efficient blades. Each change let the turbines make more power than before.

People slowly saw that wind was a renewable source of power. Coal and wood can run out, but wind never does. Burning nothing also meant no smoke filled the air.

Today, wind turbines stand together in groups called wind farms. Thousands of turbines spin quietly across hills and coasts. They turn moving air into clean power for millions of homes.

Brush connected his spinning blades to a generator, a machine built to turn mechanical motion directly into usable electrical power. Other engineers soon copied and gradually improved Brush's basic idea. Over the many decades that followed, they built considerably taller towers and longer, more efficient blades to catch more of the wind energy passing by. Each new improvement let the turbines make noticeably more power than the designs that came before them.

versions.title: The Wind Turbine: Turning Air into Power
versions.text:
For most of history, wind powered only simple tasks, such as grinding grain or pushing sails across open water. No one had harnessed wind to generate electrical power on any meaningful scale, and the idea seemed almost impossible to most people at the time, even to engineers who studied machines.

In the late 1800s, American engineer Charles Brush built an early wind-powered machine in his own backyard. His tower supported a rotor made of many thin blades arranged around a central hub. The rotor spun steadily whenever wind pushed against it with enough force and from the right direction.

Brush connected the rotor to a generator. This converted the rotor's rotation, driven by the kinetic energy of moving air, into usable electrical current. His machine supplied a modest but steady output of power for his own house, running quietly day and night, rain or clear sky.

Later engineers redesigned the blades to be more aerodynamic. This reduced drag and let the blades capture wind energy more effectively than before. These changes, along with taller towers, substantially increased each turbine's electrical output compared to Brush's early design, which now looked rather simple.

Wind offered one crucial advantage over coal: it was renewable, and it produced no smoke at all. However, wind is intermittent, meaning its output rises and falls throughout the day depending on conditions. So engineers eventually paired turbines with other power sources to keep electricity flowing reliably.

Today, thousands of turbines operate together in wind farms spread across hills and coastlines worldwide, in nearly every region of the globe, from windy plains to distant offshore waters. Their rotors continuously convert kinetic energy into clean electricity for millions of ordinary households, a true and lasting legacy of Brush's early idea and his willingness to experiment on his own.

wrong.C: Modern turbines still use rotors, just redesigned ones.
wrong.D: Modern towers are described as much taller than Brush's.

questions.stem: What does 'intermittent' mean as used in this passage?
options: Running constantly without ever stopping
Extremely powerful and strong
Completely silent and unnoticeable
Stopping and starting rather than running all the time
questions.why: The key word definition states intermittent means stopping and starting rather than running constantly.

wrong.A: This is the opposite meaning of intermittent.
wrong.B: Power level is not part of this definition.
wrong.C: Sound is unrelated to this definition.

questions.stem: How does the author structure the explanation of wind turbine history?
options: Chronologically, from early limited uses of wind to Brush's invention to modern wind farms
By comparing different religious views on energy in this situation in this situation in this situation
By presenting a debate between two named engineers
By listing safety warnings in order of importance
questions.why: The passage moves through time: early wind uses, Brush's invention, later improvements, and today's wind farms.

wrong.B: No religious views are discussed.
wrong.C: No debate between two named engineers appears.
wrong.D: No safety warnings are listed.

questions.stem: What was the effect of engineers redesigning blades to be more aerodynamic?
options: Turbines stopped converting kinetic energy into electricity
Turbines captured wind energy more effectively and produced more electrical output
Towers became shorter to save materials in this situation in this situation in this situation
Rotors were removed from the design entirely
questions.why: The passage states aerodynamic redesigns, reducing drag, substantially increased electrical output.

wrong.A: Turbines still convert kinetic energy; this process continued.
wrong.C: Towers became taller, not shorter.
wrong.D: Rotors remained central to the design.

HIGH.prompt: Explain why wind is both a useful and a tricky source of power. Use at least two key words.
checklist: I explained the advantage of wind being renewable.
I explained why wind is intermittent and what engineers did about it.
I used at least two key words correctly.
HIGH.modelAnswer: Wind is renewable, so unlike coal it never runs out, and turbines produce no smoke. The rotor's blades convert the kinetic energy of moving air into electrical output. However, wind is intermittent, meaning its output changes throughout the day, so engineers pair turbines with other power sources for reliability.

LOW.stem: What would most likely happen if there were no wind at all on a certain day?
options: The turbine's blades would not spin much
The turbine would spin even faster
The tower would grow taller
The blades would turn into sails
LOW.why: Without wind, there is no force to push the blades, so they would barely spin.

wrong.B: Less wind means less spinning, not more.
wrong.C: Towers do not grow.
wrong.D: Blades do not change into sails.

LOW.stem: Why might people today prefer wind turbines over burning coal or wood?
options: Turbines make power without smoke
Turbines are smaller than houses
Turbines use less metal
Turbines are louder
LOW.why: The passage says turbines make clean power with no smoke, unlike burning fuel.

wrong.B: Size is not discussed as an advantage.
wrong.C: Metal use is not discussed.
wrong.D: Loudness is not mentioned as a benefit.

LOW.stem: Why does the passage call the turbine machine 'a new and smart idea'?
options: Because it used wind in a new way to make power
Because no one had ever used wind before
Because it was the first machine ever built
Because it was built out of new metal
LOW.why: The passage shows wind had only been used for old tasks; using it to spin blades for power was new.

wrong.B: People had already used wind for mills and sails.
wrong.C: Other machines existed before turbines.
wrong.D: The type of metal is not discussed.

LOW.stem: What can you tell about turbines today compared to the very first ones?
options: There are now many more of them, standing together
There is now only one turbine left in the world
They no longer use wind at all
They no longer have blades
LOW.why: The passage says many tall turbines now stand together in fields, unlike the single early machines.

wrong.B: The passage says there are many turbines, not just one.
wrong.C: Turbines still use wind.
wrong.D: Turbines still have blades.

MID.stem: Based on the passage, why might Brush's invention have seemed strange to people at the time?
options: No one had ever used wind to make electrical power before
People had never seen a tower before
Electricity did not exist yet anywhere
Brush kept his invention a secret
MID.why: The passage says no one had used wind to make the kind of power in homes before Brush's experiment.

wrong.B: Towers already existed for other purposes.
wrong.C: Electricity existed; Brush's generator used it.
wrong.D: The passage does not say Brush kept it secret.

MID.stem: What can you infer about why wind farms have many turbines instead of just one?
options: More turbines together can make more total power
One turbine always breaks down quickly
Government rules require many turbines
Turbines only work in large groups
MID.why: Grouping many turbines lets a wind farm supply power to many homes, since each turbine makes a modest amount alone.

wrong.B: Breaking down is not discussed.
wrong.C: No rules are mentioned.
wrong.D: Early single turbines, like Brush's, worked alone.

MID.stem: Why does the passage mention that burning coal or wood produces smoke?
options: To show an advantage wind power has over those fuels
To explain how mills worked
To describe how turbines are built
To criticize engineers who built towers
MID.why: Mentioning smoke highlights that wind produces clean power without it, unlike coal or wood.

wrong.B: Mills are described earlier without discussing smoke.
wrong.C: Smoke is not related to how turbines are built.
wrong.D: Engineers are praised, not criticized, in the passage.

MID.stem: How does Brush's first turbine compare to turbines built decades later?
options: Later turbines had taller towers and more efficient blades
Later turbines had no blades at all
Brush's turbine made more power than later ones
Later turbines were built underground
MID.why: The passage states later engineers built taller towers and longer, more efficient blades than Brush's design.

wrong.B: All turbines, early and later, have blades.
wrong.C: Later turbines made more power, not less.
wrong.D: Turbines are not built underground.

HIGH.stem: Based on the passage, what tradeoff does wind energy present compared to coal?
options: Wind is renewable and clean but intermittent, while coal is steady but produces smoke and will run out
Wind is more expensive than coal in every situation
Coal is renewable while wind is not
Wind requires no engineering while coal requires constant engineering
HIGH.why: The passage contrasts wind's renewable, smoke-free nature with its intermittent output, versus coal's limited supply and smoke.

wrong.B: Cost comparisons are not discussed in the passage.
wrong.C: The passage states wind, not coal, is renewable.
wrong.D: Both forms of power involve engineering, as shown by Brush's and later engineers' work.

HIGH.stem: Why might the passage describe Brush's house-powering turbine before describing wind farms?
options: To show how a small personal experiment grew into a large-scale technology
Because wind farms existed before Brush's invention
Because Brush personally built every wind farm described
To prove coal power came first historically
HIGH.why: Presenting Brush's modest experiment first highlights the scale of growth from one house to worldwide wind farms.

wrong.B: The passage places Brush's invention before modern wind farms, not after.
wrong.C: Later, unnamed engineers built on his idea, not Brush himself.
wrong.D: Coal's history before wind power is not addressed.

HIGH.stem: How does the role of the generator differ from the role of the rotor in a turbine?
options: The rotor captures wind's kinetic energy through spinning, while the generator converts that motion into electrical current
The generator spins in the wind while the rotor stays still
The rotor stores electricity while the generator produces wind
They perform the exact same function in the machine
HIGH.why: The passage distinguishes the rotor's spinning motion from the generator's job of converting that motion into electrical current.

wrong.B: The passage states the rotor, not the generator, spins in the wind.
wrong.C: Neither part stores electricity or produces wind as described.
wrong.D: The two parts have distinct, different roles in the passage.

HIGH.stem: What can be inferred about the overall trend in turbine design described across the passage?
options: Turbines have steadily increased in height, blade efficiency, and electrical output over time
Turbine towers have become progressively shorter since Brush's time
Turbines have stopped using generators in recent designs
Wind turbine use has declined since the 1800s
HIGH.why: The passage consistently describes taller towers, more aerodynamic blades, and greater output as time passed.

wrong.B: Towers grew taller, not shorter, over time.
wrong.C: Generators remain essential throughout the passage.
wrong.D: The passage describes wind power growing, not declining.
